section_summary: This section documents internal and foreign political developments in Japan from mid-1932 to early 1934 surrounding the non-partisan coalition cabinet of Premier Viscount Makoto Saito following the assassination of Prime Minister Inukai. Diplomatic reporting, State Department memoranda, and news dispatches trace persistent rumors of cabinet collapse, bitter budget battles between the civil administration and the military, and repeated assassination plots by reactionary nationalist organizations. Significant personnel transitions documented include the replacement of Navy Minister Keisuke Okada by Mineo Osumi, the succession of Foreign Minister Yasuya Uchida by Koki Hirota, and the eventual resignation of War Minister Sadao Araki in favor of Senjuro Hayashi.

subfiles.about: Concluding pages of a despatch analyzing the acute domestic, economic, and diplomatic challenges confronting the newly installed Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion of Despatch No. 635 surveys severe domestic problems facing Japan, including agrarian unrest, widespread disillusionment with parliamentary government, and military hostility toward wealthy zaibatsu families. It highlights national finance difficulties, pressures for currency inflation to devalue the yen and relieve agrarian and commercial debt, and the necessity of political purification. In foreign affairs, the government confronts the forthcoming League of Nations report on Manchuria and tense relations with the Soviet Union, with military opinion under General Araki expected to dominate. Neville concludes that internal friction between the Seiyukai and Minseito parties over patronage makes the long-term survival of the Saito Cabinet highly doubtful.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 635 Regarding Domestic Problems and Political Prospects of the Saito Cabinet (Concluding Pages)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a despatch regarding the formation of a new national cabinet in Japan.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Edwin L. Neville)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 634 (filed under 894.00-P.R./54), dated June 1, 1932, from Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville. The document concerns the establishment of the Saito national coalition cabinet following the assassination of Prime Minister Inukai.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/194 (Formation of New National Cabinet in Japan)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording the formal installation of Count Yasuya Uchida as Japanese Minister of Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note recording Tokyo Telegram No. 187 of July 6, 1932, originally filed under 894.021/29. It notes that Count Yasuya Uchida was formally installed as Minister of Foreign Affairs and affirmed that Japan's foreign policy would remain unchanged.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/195 (Installation of Foreign Minister Count Yasuya Uchida)

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Count Yasuya Uchida's formal installation as Foreign Minister and his initial press conference on foreign policy.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Count Yasuya Uchida was formally installed as Minister of Foreign Affairs on the morning of July 6, 1932. In an oral interview with Japanese journalists, Uchida stated that Japan's foreign policy will remain unchanged, that Japan desires to avoid unnecessary friction with other powers, and that any blunder could lead to grave consequences. Foreign Office spokesman Shiratori confirmed the accuracy of the statements, and the telegram was repeated to Peiping.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 187 from Tokyo Regarding Installation and Policy Statement of Foreign Minister Uchida

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting Chinese Foreign Minister Dr. Lo's inquiry regarding the U.S. Government's stance on the Japanese cabinet change.
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, U.S. Consul General, Nanking
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Despatch L-255 (filed under 793.94/5423) from Willys R. Peck in Nanking, dated May 21, 1932. It records that Chinese Foreign Minister Dr. Lo Wen-kan desired to ascertain the attitude and views of the American Government regarding the cabinet change in Japan.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/196 (Chinese Inquiry Regarding Cabinet Change in Japan)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording the appointment of Lieutenant General Shigeru Honjo to the Supreme Military Council.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Telegram No. 206 of August 9, 1932 (filed under 893.01 Manchuria/379). It notes that Lieutenant General Shigeru Honjo has been relieved of his command in Manchuria and appointed to the Supreme Military Council.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/197 (Appointment of Lieutenant General Honjo to Supreme Military Council)

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting General Nobuyoshi Muto's diplomatic and military appointments in Manchuria and General Honjo's relief.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports the official announcement of General Nobuyoshi Muto's appointment to a triple position in Manchuria, designated as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary with orders to proceed to Manchuria without being formally accredited to Manchukuo. The Yomiuri Shimbun reported the appointment represents a preparatory step toward official recognition of Manchukuo, with the U.S. Military Attaché noting Muto represents aggressive military elements. Lieutenant General Honjo has been relieved of his field command and appointed a member of the Supreme Military Council.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 206 from Tokyo Regarding General Muto's Appointments in Manchuria and General Honjo's Reassignment

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording a telegram regarding General Honjo's return to Tokyo as Supreme Military Councillor.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, U.S. Minister to China, Peiping
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Peiping Telegram No. 926 of August 9, 1932 (filed under 893.01 Manchuria/378). It records reporting that General Honjo is returning to Tokyo as a Supreme Military Councillor.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/198 (General Honjo's Return to Tokyo as Supreme Military Councillor)

subfiles.about: Telegram quoting a Reuter dispatch on General Muto's installation as head of Japanese affairs in Manchuria and General Honjo's reassignment.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, U.S. Minister to China, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Minister Johnson transmits an August 8 Reuter dispatch from Tokyo announcing that General Nobuyoshi Muto was formally installed by Emperor Hirohito as supreme head of Japanese affairs in Manchuria. Muto's unified role includes Commander-in-Chief of the Japanese Army, Governor of the Kwantung Leased Territory, and special envoy to Manchukuo. General Honjo, outgoing Commander-in-Chief in Manchuria, returns to Tokyo as Supreme Military Councillor.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 926 from Peiping Regarding Installation of General Muto and Transfer of General Honjo

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording an embassy report on the appointment of Count Yasuya Uchida as Japanese Foreign Minister.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 81 (Political Report No. 56), dated July 1932. It records reporting on the appointment of Count Yasuya Uchida to head the Japanese Foreign Ministry.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/199 (Appointment of Count Yasuya Uchida as Foreign Minister)

subfiles.about: Extract from Political Report No. 56 detailing Count Uchida's resignation from the South Manchuria Railway to assume the Foreign Ministry.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: This extract reports that Count Yasuya Uchida resigned as President of the South Manchuria Railway on July 6, 1932, and assumed the post of Foreign Minister, relieving Premier Saito of holding the portfolio concurrently. Uchida's appointment had been expected for several weeks and elicited little press comment. The choice was regarded as highly agreeable to the Army and other elements advocating Japanese expansion in Manchuria.
subfiles.title: Political Report No. 56: Assumption of the Foreign Ministry by Count Yasuya Uchida (Extract)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording a report on a plot to assassinate Premier Saito, Baron Yamamoto, and Takahashi.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 111 (Political Report No. 57), dated September 1, 1932. It records information regarding an uncovered plot to assassinate Premier Viscount Makoto Saito, Home Minister Baron Tatsuo Yamamoto, and Finance Minister Korekiyo Takahashi.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/200 (Plot to Assassinate Premier Saito and Cabinet Ministers)

subfiles.about: Extract from a monthly political report detailing the police discovery of an assassination conspiracy targeting Japanese cabinet leaders.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: This page from Section II(c) of Tokyo Political Report No. 57 reports that on August 18, 1932, police announced they had uncovered a conspiracy to assassinate Prime Minister Viscount Makoto Saito and Home Minister Baron Tatsuo Yamamoto. The text on this page ends abruptly mid-sentence.
subfiles.title: Political Report No. 57: Uncovering of Assassination Plot Against Premier Saito and Cabinet Ministers (Extract, Page 21)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording a telegram regarding Count Uchida's presentation of Japan's observations on the Lytton Report.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, U.S. Minister to China, Peiping
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Peiping Telegram No. 1230 of November 3, 1932 (filed under 793.94-Commission/496). It notes Foreign Minister Count Uchida's presentation to the Cabinet regarding Japan's official observations on the Lytton Report.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/201 (Cabinet Meeting on Japanese Observations Regarding Lytton Report)

subfiles.about: Telegram quoting Reuter reporting on Foreign Minister Uchida's presentation of Japan's official response to the Lytton Commission report.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, U.S. Minister to China, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Minister Johnson transmits a Reuter dispatch from Shanghai reporting on Foreign Minister Count Uchida's presentation to the Cabinet detailing Japan's formal observations on the Lytton Report. The observations consist of five articles with an introduction and conclusion, scheduled for simultaneous publication in Tokyo and Geneva upon submission to the League of Nations. Japan's response emphatically rejects international control of Manchuria as unacceptable to Japan and Manchukuo, asserting that troop withdrawal would create severe unrest.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1230 from Peiping Regarding Cabinet Presentation of Japan's Observations on the Lytton Report

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 202 concerning political instability and speculation surrounding General Ugaki.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Laurence E. Salisbury summarizes Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 202 concerning persistent rumors of an impending Japanese cabinet change. The memorandum highlights the precarious and heterogeneous nature of the Saito Cabinet, the Seiyukai's opportunistic maneuvering, and universal dissatisfaction with the expanding military budget as the primary threat to the government. It evaluates widespread political speculation that General Kazushige Ugaki might be summoned as Premier to check military expenditures, noting contacts between House of Peers leaders and Ugaki in Chosen, Tokyo, and Osaka.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum: Rumors Regarding an Impending Cabinet Change in Japan
subfiles.to: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs / Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Comprehensive political despatch analyzing persistent rumors of a cabinet collapse, budget conflicts, and speculation regarding General Ugaki.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew analyzes rumors of an impending cabinet collapse, explaining that the Saito emergency coalition suffers from fundamental instability as a heterogeneous compromise. While the Seiyukai controls the Lower House, it hesitates to force an election that might benefit the Minseito. The main threat to the Cabinet is the unprecedented budget driven by military demands, which alarms financiers while leaving major parties without an alternative. Grew examines speculation that Governor General of Chosen Kazushige Ugaki could replace Saito to restrain military spending, but doubts Ugaki could overcome the rival Araki faction or curb popular enthusiasm for the Manchurian venture.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 202: Rumors Regarding an Impending Cabinet Change

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording an embassy political report commenting on November rumors of an impending cabinet change.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 218 (Political Report No. 60), dated December 9, 1932. It records further Embassy commentary on rumors of an impending cabinet reorganization during November.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/203 (Further Comment on Rumors of Impending Cabinet Change)

subfiles.about: Extract discussing ongoing rumors of a cabinet change, budget dissatisfaction, and the balance of power between party leaders, the Genro, and the military.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: This extract reports continued speculation during November regarding a cabinet change, heightened by the Tokyo visit of General Ugaki, Governor General of Chosen. It details political dissatisfaction with the unprecedented 1933-1934 budget and the Seiyukai's reluctance to share power with the Minseito. However, fear that a cabinet collapse might lead to a fascist regime or an unfavorable electoral outcome keeps the opposition in check. The report notes that the Genro (Prince Saionji), Count Makino, and military leaders favor retaining the Saito government until the budget passes the Diet and the Manchurian question advances.
subfiles.title: Political Report No. 60: Rumors of Cabinet Change and General Ugaki's Position (Extract)

subfiles.about: Concluding page of an extract regarding an assassination conspiracy against Premier Saito, Baron Yamamoto, and Takahashi.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: This page completes the extract begun on page 175 regarding the assassination plot against Japanese cabinet leaders. It names Home Minister Baron Tatsuo Yamamoto and Finance Minister Korekiyo Takahashi as intended victims alongside Premier Saito. The conspirators are identified as members of the Jimpukai, an extreme nationalist organization associated with the May 15, 1932 incident in which Premier Inukai was assassinated.
subfiles.title: Political Report No. 57: Assassination Plot by Jimpukai Members (Extract, Page 22)

subfiles.about: Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 254 on the routine change in the Navy Ministry.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: A memorandum by Far Eastern Affairs staff summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 254 of January 13, 1933. It notes that the resignation of Navy Minister Admiral Keisuke Okada and the appointment of Admiral Mineo Osumi was caused by Okada's ill health and constituted a routine administrative transition.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum: Resignation of Navy Minister Okada and Appointment of Osumi
subfiles.to: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Pages 2 and 3 of a despatch analyzing the implications of Admiral Okada's retirement and the background of new Navy Minister Osumi.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew explains that the Navy Minister acts primarily as the Navy's civilian representative, with policies determined collectively by naval leadership. Okada's resignation just before reaching retirement age reinforced the strict military precedent that service portfolios must be held exclusively by active-duty officers, strengthening the military's independent constitutional standing despite Premier Saito's liberal efforts to retain him. Grew transmits biographic data on Admiral Mineo Osumi, praising his diplomatic tact during the London Naval Treaty disputes and describing him as a popular officer possessing rare statesmanship.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 254: Resignation of Navy Minister Okada and Appointment of Admiral Osumi (Pages 2-3)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a despatch regarding the Saito Cabinet's anticipated resignation and Seiyukai ambitions.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 266 (filed under 894.00/464), dated January 26, 1933. It reports that the Saito Cabinet is expected to resign shortly after the Diet session, with the majority Seiyukai party hoping to receive the mandate to form a cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/205 (Anticipated Resignation of Saito Cabinet After Diet Session)

subfiles.about: Comprehensive despatch analyzing the Saito-Seiyukai agreement, political party maneuvers, and prospective cabinet alternatives.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on a political understanding reached between Premier Saito and Seiyukai president Dr. Kisaburo Suzuki stipulating that the Seiyukai will not force a cabinet crisis during the Diet session, after which the Saito Cabinet will step down. While the Seiyukai anticipates that Prince Saionji will recommend a party cabinet, public hostility toward partisan corruption remains high, making another super-party government likely. Grew assesses Kenzo Adachi's newly formed nationalist Kokumin Domei party, discounts the prospect of a fascist cabinet under Baron Hiranuma, and identifies bureaucratic maneuvers under Privy Councillor Baron Y. Kubota for a non-partisan successor cabinet. Regardless of cabinet changes, Grew notes that Japan's assertive policy regarding Manchuria and the League of Nations will remain unchanged.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 266: Political Situation in Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording an embassy report on rumors that the Saito Cabinet will resign upon termination of the Diet session.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 288 (Political Report No. 62), dated February 1933. It records that rumors of an agreement between the Saito Cabinet and the Seiyukai for the government to resign after the Diet session have become increasingly widespread.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/207 (Spread of Rumors Regarding Saito-Seiyukai Understanding)

subfiles.about: Extract discussing party calculations regarding the possible resignation of Premier Saito and the role of the Genro.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: This extract reports that rumors of an agreement for the Saito Cabinet to resign after the Diet session are spreading, though some observers believe Premier Saito's political standing is strengthening daily. The Seiyukai faces internal tension between younger radicals who want to force an immediate crisis and senior leaders who fear losing their Diet majority in an election. Meanwhile, Adachi's Kokumin Domei seeks a dissolution to increase its parliamentary representation, while the Genro's reluctance to appoint a party cabinet remains a major obstacle for the Seiyukai.
subfiles.title: Political Report No. 62: Political Maneuvering Over the Saito Cabinet's Tenure (Extract)

subfiles.about: Duplicate carbon copy of page 4 of Despatch No. 266 discussing Japanese political parties and cabinet speculations.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This single page is an exact duplicate copy of page 4 of Embassy Despatch No. 266 (Page 198). It details public skepticism toward Kenzo Adachi's Kokumin Domei, rumors of weaknesses in the Saito Cabinet, the rapid decline of fascism's vogue under Baron Hiranuma, and bureaucratic maneuvering led by Privy Councillor Baron Y. Kubota for a non-partisan cabinet.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 266: Political Situation in Japan (Duplicate Page 4)

subfiles.about: Concluding page of a State Department memorandum analyzing the foreign reassignment of militarist Foreign Office officials Shiratori and Tani.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Laurence E. Salisbury comments on press reports indicating that Toshio Shiratori has been appointed Minister to Sweden and Masayuki Tani assigned to General Muto's embassy in Changchun. Salisbury concludes that the militarist and chauvinistic faction within the Japanese Foreign Office has suffered a setback by having two of its most prominent leaders posted overseas where they can cause less disruption.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum: Personnel Changes in the Japanese Foreign Office (Page 2)
subfiles.to: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the resignation of Vice Foreign Minister Arita and the appointment of Mamoru Shigemitsu.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Hachiro Arita has resigned as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs, allegedly over disagreements with chauvinistic elements inside the Foreign Office. Former Minister to China Mamoru Shigemitsu was appointed to succeed him. In a confidential comment, Grew suggests this personnel change may signal a stronger China policy by the Japanese Foreign Office.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 99 from Tokyo Regarding Resignation of Vice Minister Arita and Appointment of Shigemitsu

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting ongoing political reporting on the durability of the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 381 (Political Report No. 65), dated May 1933. It notes continued speculation concerning the probable lifespan of the Saito Cabinet, observing that it has managed to remain in power.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/210 (Speculation Concerning Probable Life of Saito Cabinet)

subfiles.about: Extract discussing the survival of the Saito Cabinet, Takahashi's intentions, and the controversy surrounding Justice Minister Koyama.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: This extract reports continued speculation over the Saito Cabinet's longevity, noting that despite press predictions of Finance Minister Takahashi's resignation, Premier Saito appears determined to continue. It describes controversy surrounding Minister of Justice Matsukichi Koyama, who submitted his resignation following the discovery of a communist in his department. Premier Saito recommended to the Emperor that Koyama be retained, and following imperial request Koyama canceled his resignation, frustrating opposition attempts to trigger a government crisis.
subfiles.title: Political Report No. 65: Internal Political Affairs and Minister of Justice Koyama's Resignation (Extract)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Takahashi's announcement that he will remain in office, granting the Cabinet a new lease on life.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 419 (Political Report No. 66), dated June 1933. It notes that on May 22, Finance Minister Takahashi announced he would not resign, giving the Saito Cabinet renewed political stability.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/211 (Finance Minister Takahashi Decides to Remain in Office)

subfiles.about: Extract detailing Finance Minister Takahashi's decision to remain in the Cabinet and the Seiyukai's resulting disappointment.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: This extract reports that on May 22, 1933, Finance Minister Korekiyo Takahashi announced he would remain in office, dispelling widespread rumors that he would resign following the publication of the May 15 incident findings. Because Takahashi is Japan's most trusted financier, his departure would have forced the Cabinet's collapse. His decision deeply disappointed his party, the Seiyukai, which held an immediate meeting resolved to withdraw its support from the government at the earliest opportunity in order to force its own return to power.
subfiles.title: Political Report No. 66: Finance Minister Takahashi Decides to Remain (Extract)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording a despatch on the Saito Government's relations with political parties and cabinet longevity.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 497 (filed under 894.00/485), dated August 17, 1933, from Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville. It summarizes Neville's discussion of reasons for the Saito regime's continued survival and potential future political developments.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/212 (The Saito Government and the Political Parties)

subfiles.about: Extensive despatch analyzing the survival of the Saito coalition, plans to draft party leaders as ministers without portfolio, and dictatorship fears.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Neville reports that the Saito Cabinet has survived over a year despite relentless rumors of its impending collapse. The Seiyukai is eager to return to power but is restrained by pervasive public distrust of partisan corruption, reinforced by sympathetic public reactions to defendants in the ongoing May 15 incident trials. Neville describes a project to strengthen the government ahead of the difficult military budget and tax debates by drafting party presidents Dr. Kisaburo Suzuki (Seiyukai) and Baron Reijiro Wakatsuki (Minseito) as Ministers without portfolio. He warns that prominent leaders including Finance Minister Takahashi fear that public alienation from parliamentary politics could ultimately drive Japan into a feudal military dictatorship.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 497: The Saito Government and the Political Parties

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording a report on summer political developments and proposals to include party leaders in the Cabinet.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 498 (Political Report No. 68), dated August 19, 1933. It notes the summer lull in government business and revived reports that leaders of the Seiyukai and Minseito parties may join the Cabinet as ministers without portfolio.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/213 (Summer Political Lull and Proposed Cabinet Inclusion of Party Leaders)

subfiles.about: Extract discussing the summer political lull, party maneuvers, and the military's role as the foundation of the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: This extract notes that Tokyo politics have quieted during summer weather with government offices operating half-days. Reports have resurfaced that Seiyukai leader Suzuki and Minseito leader Wakatsuki may join the Cabinet as ministers without portfolio, with Suzuki showing greater willingness to cooperate despite his party's recent formal criticism of the government. The Embassy concludes that the real power preserving the Saito Government is the Army, which believes it can secure its massive 1934-1935 budget requests better from the current administration than from any alternative cabinet.
subfiles.title: Political Report No. 68: Political Situation and Proposed Coalition Expansion (Extract)

subfiles.about: Telegram (represented by corrected copy and original received copy) reporting Count Uchida's resignation as Foreign Minister and Hirota's probable appointment.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Count Yasuya Uchida resigned as Minister for Foreign Affairs on the morning of September 14, 1933, ostensibly due to ill health. Former Ambassador to Moscow Koki Hirota is prominently mentioned as his successor, although his appointment has not yet been confirmed. The file contains both the initial uncorrected transmission and a corrected copy of the telegram.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 138 from Tokyo Regarding Resignation of Foreign Minister Uchida and Proposed Succession of Hirota

subfiles.about: Telegram confirming the official appointment of Koki Hirota as Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew sends a brief follow-up telegram confirming that Koki Hirota has been officially appointed as Minister for Foreign Affairs, succeeding Count Yasuya Uchida.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 139 from Tokyo Confirming Appointment of Koki Hirota as Foreign Minister

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Chinese official and press reactions to the appointment of Koki Hirota as Japan's Foreign Minister.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, U.S. Minister to China, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Minister Johnson transmits a Reuter dispatch from Nanking regarding Chinese reactions to Koki Hirota's appointment as Japanese Foreign Minister. Chinese officials remain reticent and watchful, accepting Uchida's ill health as the real reason for retirement and expecting no major shift in Japan's China policy. However, observers note Hirota's successful settlement of Soviet-Japanese fishery disputes while Ambassador in Moscow, predicting his appointment may facilitate negotiations on Russian affairs and the Chinese Eastern Railway.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 748 from Peiping Transmitting Reuter Report on Chinese Reactions to Hirota's Appointment

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram analyzing the background of Uchida's retirement and evaluating Hirota's qualifications, temperament, and prospects.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that well-informed observers believe Count Uchida resigned due to failing health and the heavy burdens of office rather than policy disagreements, possibly anticipating a broader cabinet reorganization. Grew characterizes new Foreign Minister Koki Hirota as an experienced, conciliatory career diplomat rather than a strongman, noting his youthful ties to Mitsuru Toyama's nationalist society. Grew assesses Hirota as a safe, non-alarmist appointment who brings valuable expertise in Soviet relations and may be serving as an acceptable stop-gap prior to future cabinet changes.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 141 from Tokyo Evaluating Foreign Minister Uchida's Resignation and Hirota's Appointment

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram reporting Hirota's personal pledge to prioritize improving relations with the United States.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on his initial diplomatic reception with new Foreign Minister Koki Hirota on September 18, 1933. Hirota stated that his appointment came as a complete surprise and declared that his foremost preoccupation while in office would be fostering better relations with the United States, calling this the primary reason he agreed to accept the post.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 144 from Tokyo Regarding Ambassador Grew's Initial Meeting with Foreign Minister Hirota

subfiles.about: Comprehensive biographical and political study of incoming Foreign Minister Koki Hirota, assessing his career, diplomatic orientation, and selection.
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman (FE:EHD/ZMK), Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs provides a thorough review of Koki Hirota's diplomatic background upon his appointment as Foreign Minister succeeding Count Uchida. The memorandum traces his career from Tokyo Imperial University through assignments in Washington, the European and American Affairs Bureau, Minister to The Hague, and Ambassador to Moscow where he negotiated the 1924 treaty and resolved fisheries disputes. It discounts press assertions that Hirota is an extreme nationalist, observing that while he enjoys the confidence of the military, his career demonstrates moderate, progressive statesmanship and a friendly disposition toward the United States.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum: Change of Ministers for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Newspaper reports on Count Uchida's resignation, Hirota's succession, and prospects for a complete cabinet transformation.
subfiles.from: The Associated Press / The New York Times
subfiles.summary: An Associated Press dispatch from Tokyo reports Count Uchida's resignation due to failing health, asserting that reactionary pressure favored Koki Hirota, whom it describes as a staunch nationalist closely connected to army cliques. A companion special cable predicts a complete cabinet reorganization before the end of the year, explaining that the elderly ministers seek to retire and suggesting Japan is shifting toward a non-partisan authoritarian government modeled on pre-war imperial Germany.
subfiles.title: New York Times Clipping: 'Uchida Quits as Japan's Foreign Minister; Hirota, Successor, Even More Nationalistic'

subfiles.about: Clipping reporting Uchida's retirement, Hirota's appointment, and War Minister Araki's speech citing U.S. naval threats.
subfiles.from: The Associated Press / The Baltimore Sun
subfiles.summary: This clipping reports Count Yasuya Uchida's resignation as Foreign Minister and the selection of Koki Hirota, reviewing Uchida's past diplomatic service in Washington, St. Petersburg, and Vienna. It covers a major address by War Minister General Sadao Araki before the Supreme War Council, in which Araki pointed to American sympathy and financial assistance to China—including a $50,000,000 wheat and cotton loan—and the presence of the U.S. Atlantic Fleet in the Pacific as critical national defense emergencies requiring substantial increases in military budgets.
subfiles.title: Baltimore Sun Clipping: 'Foreign Minister of Japan Resigns / War Head Refers to U.S. Fleet'

subfiles.about: Clippings reporting Hirota's imperial installation and the establishment of a Japanese-controlled buffer zone in North China.
subfiles.from: United Press / Washington Herald
subfiles.summary: United Press dispatches report the imperial installation of Foreign Minister Koki Hirota at Hayama Palace following Count Uchida's sudden resignation, reviewing Uchida's career and his leadership during Japan's withdrawal from the League of Nations. A companion dispatch from Peiping reports that Japan has established a demilitarized 'buffer state' in North China below the Great Wall, where Chinese police under rebel General Li Chi-chun take orders from Manchukuo authorities, an arrangement condemned by Chinese press as a humiliating national surrender.
subfiles.title: Washington Herald Clipping: 'New Official Will Assume Duties Today / Japan Buffer State Set Up in North China'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Under Secretary Phillips' conversation with Japanese Ambassador Debuchi regarding Foreign Minister Hirota.
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing a memorandum of conversation (filed under 701.9411/768) recorded by Under Secretary of State William Phillips on September 28, 1933. The memorandum records a discussion with Japanese Ambassador Katsuji Debuchi concerning newly appointed Foreign Minister Koki Hirota.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/220 (Conversation Between Under Secretary Phillips and Japanese Ambassador on Hirota)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording an embassy telegram on acute cabinet divisions over military budgets.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Telegram No. 156 of October 11, 1933 (filed under 894.00/488). It records ongoing reporting of severe internal dissension within the Japanese Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/221 (Continued Reports of Serious Disagreements in Japanese Cabinet)

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram reporting Hirota's alignment with Takahashi against military budget demands and the danger of an army coup.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports serious cabinet discord as new Foreign Minister Koki Hirota allies with Finance Minister Takahashi to resist inflated army and navy appropriation demands. Leveraging his past credibility with reactionary and nationalist groups, Hirota is attempting to convince them that Japan faces no immediate danger and that international ill-will from excessive military spending outweighs security gains. Grew warns that if Hirota and Takahashi prevail, frustrated militarists may launch a coup d'état, and notes that Premier Saito must either resolve these internal factions or resign before the Diet convenes in December.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 156 from Tokyo Regarding Cabinet Clashes Over Military Appropriations and Coup Risks

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording a telegram analyzing the resignation of War Minister Araki and the appointment of General Hayashi.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note cross-referencing Tokyo Telegram No. 15 of January 23, 1934 (filed under 894.00/502). It records Ambassador Grew's report analyzing the reasons for General Sadao Araki's resignation as Minister of War, political reactions, and the policies expected from the new War Minister, General Senjuro Hayashi.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.002/222 (Resignation of War Minister Araki and Appointment of General Hayashi)
